\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

A compressed file is meaningless without a decompressor, and the decompressor is
shared: one program must serve all inputs. A decompressor specialised to a class of
data encodes prior knowledge and therefore produces shorter files on that class. The
\emph{price of universality} is the number of bits per message that a single shared
scheme must waste relative to a scheme specialised to the true source.

Fix a finite message space $X$ and a family of sources
$\Sc=\{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, $\Theta$ finite. A \emph{coding distribution} is a
probability distribution $q$ on $X$; the ideal codeword length it assigns to $x$ is
$\log_2(1/q(x))$, and by the Kraft inequality this correspondence between coding
distributions and prefix codes is essentially exact (Section~\ref{sec:oper}). The
redundancy of $q$ against $p_\theta$ is the relative entropy
\[
\Dv{p_\theta}{q}=\sum_{x\in X}p_\theta(x)\log_2\frac{p_\theta(x)}{q(x)},
\]
the average number of bits per message wasted by coding $p_\theta$-data with $q$. The
price of universality is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:minimax}
R^\star(\Sc)=\min_{q}\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\Dv{p_\theta}{q}.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Two prices}

\emph{Worst case (pointwise).} Requiring closeness to the best-fitting member on
\emph{every individual message} gives the minimax value $\log_2 C_{\Sc}$ with
$C_{\Sc}=\sum_x\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$ the \emph{Shtarkov sum}, attained by the
normalized maximum-likelihood distribution.

\emph{Average case (Bayes).} Requiring only small expected redundancy under each
source gives \eqref{eq:minimax}, whose value we prove to be the channel capacity $C$
of the family. We show $C\le\log_2 C_{\Sc}$ always, with an explicit family where the
gap is $\tfrac14\log_2 3$ bits.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item An exact, non-asymptotic, minimax-theorem-free proof of the
        redundancy--capacity theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:rc}), via prior perturbation

  \item Structural theory of the capacity: positivity, monotonicity, additivity,

  \item Uniqueness of the optimal universal coding distribution

  \item An exact chain rule for coarse-grainings and the characterisation of free

\section{Setup and notation}

\begin{definition}[Source class]
A \emph{source class} $\Sc$ on a finite set $X$ indexed by a finite non-empty set
$\Theta$ assigns to each $\theta$ a probability vector $p_\theta:X\to\Rb_{\ge0}$ with
$\sum_x p_\theta(x)=1$. It is \emph{strictly positive} if $p_\theta(x)>0$ for all
$\theta,x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Entropy, divergence]
For probability vectors $p,q$ with $q>0$,
$H(p)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)$ and $\Dv{p}{q}=\sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$,
with $0\log_2 0=0$. Gibbs' inequality gives $\Dv{p}{q}\ge0$, with equality iff $p=q$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Prior, mixture, Bayes redundancy]
A \emph{prior} is $w\in\Delta(\Theta)=\{w\ge 0:\sum_\theta w_\theta=1\}$. Its
\emph{Bayes mixture} is $m_w(x)=\sum_\theta w_\theta p_\theta(x)$ and its \emph{Bayes
redundancy} is $I(w)=\sum_\theta w_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{m_w}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Capacity, Shtarkov sum]
$C=C(\Sc)=\sup_{w\in\Delta(\Theta)}I(w)$;
$C_{\Sc}=\sum_x\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$ and
$\nml(x)=\max_\theta p_\theta(x)/C_{\Sc}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Compensation identity]\label{lem:comp}
For every prior $w$ and every strictly positive $q$ with $\sum_x q(x)\le1$,
\[
\sum_\theta w_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{q}=I(w)+\Dv{m_w}{q}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $\log_2(p_\theta/q)=\log_2(p_\theta/m_w)+\log_2(m_w/q)$, multiply by
$w_\theta p_\theta(x)$ and sum; the second block sums to
$\sum_x m_w(x)\log_2(m_w(x)/q(x))$ since $\sum_\theta w_\theta p_\theta=m_w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mutual-information form]\label{lem:mi}
If $\Sc$ is strictly positive and $w\in\Delta(\Theta)$ then
\[
I(w)=H(m_w)-\sum_\theta w_\theta H(p_\theta),
\]
so $I(w)$ is the mutual information between the source index (distributed as $w$) and
the emitted message, and $C$ is the Shannon capacity of the channel $\theta\mapsto x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $\Dv{p_\theta}{m_w}=\sum_x p_\theta\log_2 p_\theta-\sum_x p_\theta\log_2 m_w$,
weight by $w_\theta$ and sum. The first block gives $-\sum_\theta w_\theta H(p_\theta)$;
exchanging summation order in the second turns $\sum_\theta w_\theta p_\theta(x)$ into
$m_w(x)$, giving $+H(m_w)$.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:mi} exhibits $I$ as a \emph{continuous} function of $w$, which is what
compactness needs.

\section{Two analytic tools}

\begin{lemma}[Vanishing first order]\label{lem:firstorder}
Let $a,K\in\Rb$ with $K\ge0$. If $a\le tK$ for every $t\in(0,1]$, then $a\le0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $a>0$, take $t=\min\{1,\ a/(2(K+1))\}>0$; then $tK\le a/2<a$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\chi^2$ bound]\label{thm:chi2}
Let $a$ be a probability vector and $b$ a strictly positive probability vector on $X$.
Then
\[
\Dv{a}{b}\;\le\;\frac{1}{\ln 2}\sum_x\frac{(a(x)-b(x))^2}{b(x)}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By $\ln u\le u-1$ with $u=a(x)/b(x)$,
$a(x)\ln\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}\le\frac{a(x)^2}{b(x)}-a(x)$. Summing and using
$\sum_x a(x)=1$ gives $\sum_x a\ln\frac{a}{b}\le\sum_x\frac{a^2}{b}-1$. Finally
$\sum_x\frac{(a-b)^2}{b}=\sum_x\frac{a^2}{b}-2+1=\sum_x\frac{a^2}{b}-1$. Divide by
$\ln 2$.
\end{proof}

The point is \emph{quadratic} control: if $a-b=t\,v$ then the bound is $O(t^2)$.

\section{The redundancy--capacity theorem}

Throughout, $\Sc$ is strictly positive and $\Theta\ne\emptyset$.

\begin{lemma}[Existence of an optimal prior]\label{lem:exists}
The supremum defining $C$ is attained: there is $w^\star\in\Delta(\Theta)$ with
$I(w^\star)=C$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:mi}, $I$ agrees on $\Delta(\Theta)$ with a continuous function;
$\Delta(\Theta)$ is compact and non-empty; apply the extreme value theorem.
\end{proof}

Note that strict positivity forces $m_w>0$ for every $w\in\Delta(\Theta)$.

\begin{theorem}[Saddle point]\label{thm:saddle}
Let $w^\star$ maximise $I$ over $\Delta(\Theta)$ and put $m^\star=m_{w^\star}$. Then
\[
\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}\;\le\;I(w^\star)=C \qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $\theta_0$ and for $t\in(0,1]$ set $w_t=(1-t)w^\star+t\delta_{\theta_0}$, whose
mixture is $m_t=(1-t)m^\star+t\,p_{\theta_0}$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:perturb}
m_t-m^\star=t\,(p_{\theta_0}-m^\star).
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:comp} with prior $w_t$ and coding distribution $m^\star$ gives
$\sum_\theta (w_t)_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}=I(w_t)+\Dv{m_t}{m^\star}$. The
left-hand side equals $(1-t)I(w^\star)+t\Dv{p_{\theta_0}}{m^\star}$, again by
Lemma~\ref{lem:comp} (with $w^\star$, where $\Dv{m^\star}{m^\star}=0$). Maximality
gives $I(w_t)\le I(w^\star)$, hence
\[
t\left(\Dv{p_{\theta_0}}{m^\star}-I(w^\star)\right)\le \Dv{m_t}{m^\star}.
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:chi2} and \eqref{eq:perturb}, $\Dv{m_t}{m^\star}\le t^2 V/\ln 2$
with $V=\sum_x (p_{\theta_0}(x)-m^\star(x))^2/m^\star(x)\ge0$. Divide by $t$ and apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:firstorder} with $K=V/\ln2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Achievability]\label{cor:ach}
The distribution $q=m^\star$ is strictly positive, sums to $1$, and satisfies
$\Dv{p_\theta}{q}\le C$ for every $\theta$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Redundancy--capacity theorem]\label{thm:rc}
For a finite strictly positive source class,
$\min_q\max_\theta \Dv{p_\theta}{q}=C$. Explicitly: \textup{(i)} $m^\star$ satisfies
$\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}\le C$ for all $\theta$; \textup{(ii)} for every strictly
positive $q$ with $\sum_x q(x)\le1$ there is $\theta$ with $\Dv{p_\theta}{q}\ge C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(i) is Corollary~\ref{cor:ach}. For (ii), Lemma~\ref{lem:comp} with $w^\star$ gives
$\sum_\theta w^\star_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{q}=C+\Dv{m^\star}{q}\ge C$, so some term is
at least $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Verification criterion]\label{thm:verif}
If some strictly positive $q$ with $\sum_x q(x)\le1$ satisfies $\Dv{p_\theta}{q}\le c$
for all $\theta$, then $C\le c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$C\le C+\Dv{m^\star}{q}=\sum_\theta w^\star_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{q}\le c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Equalizer property]\label{thm:equal}
If $w^\star$ is capacity-achieving and $w^\star_\theta>0$, then
$\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}=C$ exactly.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All terms are $\le C$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle}; if one with positive weight were
strictly smaller, then $C=I(w^\star)=\sum_\theta w^\star_\theta\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}<C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of the optimal code]\label{thm:unique}
If $w_1,w_2$ are both capacity-achieving priors then $m_{w_1}=m_{w_2}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:saddle} at $w_2$, $\Dv{p_\theta}{m_{w_2}}\le C$ for all $\theta$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:comp} with prior $w_1$ and $q=m_{w_2}$ gives
$C+\Dv{m_{w_1}}{m_{w_2}}\le C$, so $\Dv{m_{w_1}}{m_{w_2}}=0$ and strict Gibbs gives
equality of the mixtures.
\end{proof}

Thus the optimal universal decompressor is canonical, not an artefact of the
optimisation.

\section{First structural consequences}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity]\label{thm:pos}
If $p_{\theta_1}\ne p_{\theta_2}$ for some $\theta_1,\theta_2$, then $C>0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $C=0$ then $I(u)=0$ for the uniform prior $u$, so every $\Dv{p_\theta}{m_u}=0$ and
strict Gibbs forces all $p_\theta=m_u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-part bound]\label{thm:twopart}
$C\le\log_2|\Theta|$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:verif} to $q=m_u$: since $m_u(x)\ge p_\theta(x)/|\Theta|$, we
get $\Dv{p_\theta}{m_u}\le\log_2|\Theta|$ termwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Average $\le$ worst case]\label{thm:avgworst}
$C\le\log_2 C_{\Sc}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:verif} to $q=\nml$: for all $\theta,x$,
$p_\theta(x)/\nml(x)\le C_{\Sc}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]\label{thm:mono}
If $\Tc=\{p_{f(\theta')}\}_{\theta'\in\Theta'}$ is a subfamily of $\Sc$ then
$C(\Tc)\le C(\Sc)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The optimal code for $\Sc$ is within $C(\Sc)$ of every source of $\Tc$; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:verif}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Distinguishable classes]\label{thm:disj}
If there are pairwise disjoint $A_\theta\subseteq X$ with
$\sum_{x\in A_\theta}p_\theta(x)\ge1-\delta$ for all $\theta$, then
\[
(1-\delta)\log_2|\Theta|-4\;\le\;C\;\le\;\log_2|\Theta|.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The upper bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:twopart}. For the lower bound, any coding
distribution $q$ has $\sum_\theta q(A_\theta)\le1$, so some $\theta$ has
$q(A_\theta)\le1/|\Theta|$; the two-cell data-processing estimate on
$\{A_\theta,A_\theta^c\}$ gives $\Dv{p_\theta}{q}\ge(1-\delta)\log_2|\Theta|-4$. Apply
this to the optimal $q$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:ach}.
\end{proof}

\section{Operational form: real codes, real bits}\label{sec:oper}

A length function $\ell:X\to\Nb$ is \emph{Kraft compliant} if $\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)}\le1$;
such $\ell$ are exactly the length functions of prefix-free binary codes. Write
$L(p,\ell)=\sum_x p(x)\ell(x)$.

\begin{theorem}[Converse in code lengths]
For every Kraft-compliant $\ell$ there is $\theta$ with
$L(p_\theta,\ell)\ge H(p_\theta)+C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $q(x)=2^{-\ell(x)}$; then $L(p,\ell)=H(p)+\Dv{p}{q}$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:rc}(ii).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Achievability in code lengths]
The Shannon code $\ell(x)=\lceil\log_2(1/m^\star(x))\rceil$ of the capacity mixture is
Kraft compliant and satisfies $L(p_\theta,\ell)\le H(p_\theta)+C+1$ for every $\theta$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$2^{-\ell(x)}\le m^\star(x)$ gives Kraft compliance; $\ell(x)<\log_2(1/m^\star(x))+1$
gives $L(p_\theta,\ell)\le H(p_\theta)+\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}+1\le H(p_\theta)+C+1$.
\end{proof}

Thus the minimax expected redundancy of prefix codes is bracketed between $C$ and
$C+1$ bits per message; the slack is integer-length rounding.

\section{Symmetry, products, and the cost of model selection}

\subsection{Additivity over independent blocks}

For classes $\Sc$ on $X$ and $\Tc$ on $Y$, the product class $\Sc\otimes\Tc$ on
$X\times Y$ has sources $(x,y)\mapsto p_\theta(x)r_\psi(y)$.

\begin{theorem}[Additivity]\label{thm:tensor}
For strictly positive $\Sc,\Tc$, $\;C(\Sc\otimes\Tc)=C(\Sc)+C(\Tc)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Divergence is additive on products,
$\Dv{p\otimes r}{a\otimes b}=\Dv{p}{a}+\Dv{r}{b}$. For $\le$, apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:verif} to $m^\star_{\Sc}\otimes m^\star_{\Tc}$. For $\ge$, the
product of capacity-achieving priors has Bayes redundancy
$I(w^\star)+I(v^\star)=C(\Sc)+C(\Tc)$.
\end{proof}

The direction $\le$ says there is \emph{no universality discount across independent
data}; it is immediate from the saddle point.

\subsection{Transitive symmetry and unknown-offset classes}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetric classes]\label{thm:sym}
Suppose a group $G$ acts on $X$ and on $\Theta$ by bijections with
$p_{g\cdot\theta}(g\cdot x)=p_\theta(x)$, transitively on $\Theta$. Then the uniform
prior is capacity-achieving and $C=\Dv{p_\theta}{m_u}$ for every $\theta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Unknown-offset class]
For a finite abelian group $A$ and a probability distribution $p_0$ on $A$, the
\emph{shift class} is $\Sc_{p_0}=\{p_\theta\}_{\theta\in A}$ with
$p_\theta(x)=p_0(x-\theta)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closed forms]\label{thm:shift}
If $p_0>0$ then
\[
C(\Sc_{p_0})=\log_2|A|-H(p_0),\qquad \log_2 C_{\Sc_{p_0}}=\log_2|A|-H_\infty(p_0),
\]
where $H_\infty(p_0)=-\log_2\max_a p_0(a)$. Consequently
\[
\log_2 C_{\Sc_{p_0}}-C(\Sc_{p_0})=H(p_0)-H_\infty(p_0)\ \ge 0 .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The translation group acts transitively and compatibly, so Theorem~\ref{thm:sym}
applies; the uniform mixture of all translates is the uniform law $u_A$, and
$\Dv{p_0}{u_A}=\log_2|A|-H(p_0)$. For the Shtarkov sum,
$\max_\theta p_0(x-\theta)=\max_a p_0(a)$ for every $x$, so
$C_{\Sc}=|A|\max_a p_0(a)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[An explicit strict gap]\label{ex:bias34}
Let $A=\mathbb Z/2$ and $p_0=(3/4,1/4)$, i.e.\ the class
$\{(3/4,1/4),(1/4,3/4)\}$. Then
\[
C=\tfrac34\log_2 3-1\approx0.1887,\qquad \log_2 C_{\Sc}=\log_2 3-1\approx0.5850,
\]
with gap exactly $\tfrac14\log_2 3\approx0.3962$ bits. The two prices of universality
are genuinely different quantities.
\end{example}

\subsection{The exact cost of model selection}

Let $\Tc_1,\dots,\Tc_K$ be classes on the same message space and let
$\Sigma=\bigsqcup_i\Tc_i$ be their disjoint union as a single class.

\begin{theorem}[Model-selection sandwich]\label{thm:sigma}
If $C(\Tc_i)\le B$ for all $i$, then
$\max_i C(\Tc_i)\le C(\Sigma)\le B+\log_2 K$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The lower bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:mono}. For the upper bound take
$q=\frac1K\sum_i q_i$ with $q_i$ optimal for $\Tc_i$; then $q\ge q_i/K$ pointwise, so
$\Dv{p}{q}\le\Dv{p}{q_i}+\log_2 K\le B+\log_2 K$ for every source $p$ of $\Tc_i$;
apply Theorem~\ref{thm:verif}.
\end{proof}

Equivalently: \emph{the total number of bits that specialisation can move from the
message into the shared decompressor is at most $\log_2(\text{number of classes})$.}

\section{Parses: data processing, sufficiency, and the price of a front end}\label{sec:parse}

Practical compressors see a \emph{parse} $f(x)$ for a map $f:X\to Y$ into a finite
set. Write $f_*p(y)=\sum_{x:f(x)=y}p(x)$ and $f_*\Sc=\{f_*p_\theta\}$.

\begin{theorem}[Data processing]\label{thm:dp}
$\Dv{f_*p}{f_*q}\le\Dv{p}{q}$ for $p,q>0$, and consequently
$C(f_*\Sc)\le C(\Sc)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The log-sum inequality applied fibre by fibre; the capacity statement follows by
taking suprema over priors.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Parse defect]
For strictly positive $p,q$ and $f:X\to Y$,
\[
D(p\|q\mid f)=\sum_{y\in Y}\ \sum_{x:f(x)=y} p(x)\,
\log_2\frac{p(x)/f_*p(y)}{q(x)/f_*q(y)},
\]
the divergence between the conditional laws of $p$ and $q$ inside the fibres of $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Chain rule]\label{thm:chain}
For strictly positive $p,q$,
$\Dv{p}{q}=\Dv{f_*p}{f_*q}+D(p\|q\mid f)$, and $D(p\|q\mid f)\ge0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inside the fibre over $y$ write
$\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}=\log_2\frac{f_*p(y)}{f_*q(y)}+\log_2\frac{p(x)/f_*p(y)}{q(x)/f_*q(y)}$
and sum, using $\sum_{x:f(x)=y}p(x)=f_*p(y)$. Non-negativity of each fibre term is
Gibbs' inequality for the two conditional laws.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Price of a parse]\label{thm:parseprice}
There is a capacity-achieving prior $w^\star$ with
\[
C(f_*\Sc)\;\le\;C(\Sc)\;\le\;C(f_*\Sc)+\sum_\theta w^\star_\theta\,
D\!\left(p_\theta\,\middle\|\,m_{w^\star}\ \middle|\ f\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Free front ends are exactly sufficient statistics]\label{thm:suff}
Let $\{p_\theta\}$ and $m$ be strictly positive. Then
$D(p_\theta\|m\mid f)=0$ for every $\theta$ if and only if there are
$g_\theta:Y\to\Rb_{>0}$ with $p_\theta(x)=g_\theta(f(x))\,m(x)$ for all $\theta,x$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) The factor $g_\theta(y)$ is constant on the fibre and cancels against
the pushforward, so the conditional laws coincide and every fibre term vanishes.
($\Rightarrow$) A zero sum of non-negative fibre terms forces each to vanish; strict
Gibbs forces $p_\theta(x)/f_*p_\theta(f(x))=m(x)/f_*m(f(x))$, i.e.\ the Fisher--Neyman
factorisation with $g_\theta(y)=f_*p_\theta(y)/f_*m(y)$.
\end{proof}

In slogan form: \emph{the price of universality is a function of the sufficient
statistic alone}, and every non-sufficient parse pays exactly for what it discards.

\section{Rates: how the price grows with message length}\label{sec:rates}

\begin{lemma}[Counting bound]\label{lem:count}
For any strictly positive class on a message space $X$, $C\le\log_2|X|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$C_{\Sc}\le|X|$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:avgworst}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Memoryless families}

Let $A$ be a finite alphabet, $X=A^n$, and $p_t(x)=\prod_{i<n}t(x_i)$. The type map
$\tau:A^n\to\Nb^A$ (vector of symbol counts) satisfies
$p_t(x)=\prod_{a}t(a)^{\tau(x)_a}$, so it is a sufficient statistic and
$C(\tau_*\Sc)=C(\Sc)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:suff}. Since $|\tau(A^n)|\le(n+1)^{|A|}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:count} gives:

\begin{theorem}[Memoryless rate]\label{thm:iid}
For every finite family of strictly positive memoryless sources over $A$ on messages
of length $n$,
\[
C\;\le\;|A|\,\log_2(n+1),
\]
uniformly in the number of sources. For $A=\{0,1\}$ the count of ones is already
sufficient, so $C\le\log_2(n+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Markov families}

\begin{theorem}[Markov rate]\label{thm:markov}
For every finite family of strictly positive first-order Markov laws on $A^n$,
\[
C\;\le\;\log_2|A|+|A|^2\log_2(n+1).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The pair (first symbol, matrix of transition counts) is sufficient and its range has
at most $|A|(n+1)^{|A|^2}$ elements; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:suff} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:count}.
\end{proof}

The multiplier $|A|^2$ is the number of free parameters of the class: this is the
Rissanen shape, here as a clean non-asymptotic bound.

\subsection{Smoothing}

For $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ let $p^{(\varepsilon)}_\theta=(1-\varepsilon)p_\theta+\varepsilon u_X$.

\begin{theorem}[Smoothed distinguishable classes]\label{thm:smooth}
If the $A_\theta$ are pairwise disjoint with $p_\theta(A_\theta)=1$, then
\[
(1-\varepsilon)\log_2|\Theta|-4\;\le\;C\big(\Sc^{(\varepsilon)}\big)\;\le\;\log_2|\Theta|.
\]
\end{theorem}

Applied to the constant-composition class of $n$-bit files ($|\Theta|=n+1$) this gives
$(1-\varepsilon)\log_2(n+1)-4\le C\le\log_2(n+1)$: for this rich binary class,
$\log_2 n$ is the exact order.

\subsection{A genuine one-parameter lower bound: the Bernoulli packing}

Fix $n$ and a scale $k$ with $k^2\le n$ (intended: $k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$).
Consider the Bernoulli parameters
\[
t_j=\frac{4j+2}{k},\qquad 0\le j<\lfloor k/4\rfloor ,
\]
and the i.i.d.\ laws they induce on $\{0,1\}^n$. Let $N(x)$ be the number of ones.

\begin{lemma}[Moments]\label{lem:moments}
Under the product Bernoulli$(t)$ law on $\{0,1\}^n$,
$\Ex[N]=nt$ and $\Ex[(N-nt)^2]=nt(1-t)\le n/4$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $n$ via the splitting bijection
$\{0,1\}^{n+1}\cong\{0,1\}\times\{0,1\}^n$; the expectations are finite sums, so no
measure theory is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Chebyshev window]\label{lem:cheb}
With $r=2n/k$ and $k^2\le n$,
$\Pr\big[|N-nt|<2n/k\big]\ge 1-\frac{nk^2}{16n^2}\ge\frac{15}{16}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Disjointness]\label{lem:disjwin}
The windows $W_j=\{x:|N(x)-nt_j|<2n/k\}$ are pairwise disjoint: consecutive means
$nt_j=(n/k)(4j+2)$ are $4n/k$ apart while windows have half-width $2n/k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli bracket]\label{thm:bern}
For $k^2\le n$ and $k\ge8$ the family $\{p_{t_j}\}_{j<\lfloor k/4\rfloor}$ satisfies
$\tfrac{15}{16}\log_2\lfloor k/4\rfloor-4\le C$. Taking $k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$, for
every $n\ge64$,
\[
\tfrac{15}{32}\log_2 n-8\;\le\;C\;\le\;\log_2(n+1).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Lemmas~\ref{lem:cheb} and~\ref{lem:disjwin} make $\{W_j\}$ approximately disjoint with
$\delta=1/16$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:disj} and, for the upper bound,
Theorem~\ref{thm:iid} in the binary case. The stated form follows from
$\lfloor\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor/4\rfloor\ge\sqrt n/8$ for $n\ge64$.
\end{proof}

So the Rissanen constant of a one-parameter family --- classically $1/2$ --- is
bracketed between $15/32$ and $1$, with explicit constants at every finite $n$.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Blahut--Arimoto: computing the price.}
Start from the uniform prior $w^{(0)}$; given $w^{(s)}$, form
$m^{(s)}=\sum_\theta w^{(s)}_\theta p_\theta$ and
$d^{(s)}_\theta=\Dv{p_\theta}{m^{(s)}}$, then set
$w^{(s+1)}_\theta\propto w^{(s)}_\theta 2^{d^{(s)}_\theta}$. Then
$I(w^{(s)})\uparrow C$ and $\max_\theta d^{(s)}_\theta\downarrow C$, so
$[\,I(w^{(s)}),\max_\theta d^{(s)}_\theta\,]$ is a certified enclosure of $C$ at every
step (upper certificate: Theorem~\ref{thm:verif}). Cost $O(|\Theta||X|)$ per iteration.

\paragraph{The optimal universal code.}
Output $m^\star$ and encode with the Shannon code (in practice, arithmetic coding
against $m^\star$, which removes the $+1$).

\paragraph{Auditing a front end.}
Compute
$\Delta(f)=\sum_\theta w^\star_\theta\left(\Dv{p_\theta}{m^\star}-\Dv{f_*p_\theta}{f_*m^\star}\right)$.
By Theorems~\ref{thm:chain}--\ref{thm:suff}, $\Delta(f)=0$ iff $f$ is sufficient, and
otherwise $\Delta(f)$ is the number of bits per message the front end discards.

\section{Discussion: is specialisation worth it?}

The price of universality of a $d$-parameter family on messages of length $n$ is
$\Theta(\log n)$ bits \emph{in total}; merging $K$ specialised classes costs at most
$\log_2 K$ bits; the price is additive over independent blocks, hence cannot be
amortised by bundling; and it is strictly positive but bounded by $\log_2|\Theta|$.

\textbf{Verdict.} Specialised decompressors can move at most $O(\log n)$ bits out of
the message and into the shared decompressor. For a one-megabyte file from a modest
model class, the entire theoretical prize is tens of bits. Specialisation pays in three
regimes: (i) very short messages, where $\log_2 n$ is a substantial fraction of the
file; (ii) many independently coded records, where the toll is paid once per block;
(iii) large model families, where the toll scales with the parameter count.

\textbf{Constructive redirection.} Since the price depends only on the sufficient
statistic, the useful question is not ``should I ship more decompressors?'' but ``is my
front end sufficient?''. A sufficient parse is free; a non-sufficient one has an
explicit, computable price.

\textbf{Relation to classical results.} Theorem~\ref{thm:rc} is the
redundancy--capacity theorem of Gallager, Ryabko and Davisson; the contribution here is
a non-asymptotic proof that avoids the minimax theorem and therefore yields the
equalizer property, the verification criterion, uniqueness and additivity as immediate
corollaries. Theorems~\ref{thm:iid}--\ref{thm:markov} are non-asymptotic forms of
Rissanen's $\frac d2\log n$ rate obtained from sufficiency plus counting, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:bern} supplies the matching lower half for $d=1$.

\section{Future directions}

Two exact theories now sit side by side: the worst-case minimax redundancy
$\log_2 C_{\Sc}$ and the average-case minimax redundancy $C$; they are ordered and
provably distinct. Natural next steps:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Close the Rissanen constant.} Replace the Chebyshev tail by a
        Bernstein or exact binomial estimate to move the lower constant from $15/32$
        towards $1/2$.
  \item \textbf{Multi-parameter packings.} Extend the packing from the one-parameter
        Bernoulli family to $d$-parameter memoryless and Markov families, targeting
        $\tfrac d2\log_2 n-O(d)$.
  \item \textbf{The Jeffreys prior.} Identify the capacity-achieving prior
        asymptotically with the Jeffreys prior, making the unique optimal
        decompressor explicit.
  \item \textbf{Sequential codes.} Extend the exact theory to online prediction via
        the per-symbol form of the compensation identity.
  \item \textbf{Practical parse audits.} Compute $\Delta(f)$ for the parses used by
        real codecs and measure their distance from sufficiency.
  \item \textbf{Beyond finite spaces.} Extend the perturbation proof to countable and
        continuous message spaces.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

The price of universality is the capacity of the channel that carries the identity of
the source to the observed message. That identification --- proved here exactly,
non-asymptotically, and by an elementary perturbation --- makes the optimal universal
decompressor unique and canonical, makes the price additive, positive, monotone and
computable, prices front ends by their sufficiency defect, and reduces the practical
question of specialised decompressors to a logarithm.

This self-contained script demonstrates, numerically, the main results of

on a finite message space X.  A *coding distribution* q is a probability

    D(p_theta || q) = sum_x p_theta(x) log2( p_theta(x) / q(x) )   bits per message.

The price of universality is the minimax value  min_q max_theta D(p_theta || q).

Main theorem (redundancy-capacity theorem)
------------------------------------------
    min_q max_theta D(p_theta || q)  =  C  :=  max_w  I(w),
    I(w) = sum_theta w_theta D(p_theta || m_w),   m_w = sum_theta w_theta p_theta.

I(w) is the mutual information between the source index and the message, so C is
the Shannon capacity of the channel theta -> x.

What this script checks
-----------------------
 1. Blahut-Arimoto computation of C, with a certified two-sided bracket.
 2. The saddle point / equalizer property of the optimal prior.
 3. Uniqueness of the optimal Bayes mixture (from two different starting priors).
 4. Closed form for unknown-offset classes:  C = log2|A| - H(p0),
    worst case = log2|A| - Hmin(p0), gap = H(p0) - Hmin(p0).
 5. The explicit Bernoulli(3/4) two-source class: C = (3/4)log2 3 - 1,
    worst case = log2 3 - 1, gap = (1/4) log2 3.
 6. Additivity of the capacity over independent blocks.
 7. Model-selection sandwich: merging K classes costs at most log2 K bits.
 8. Data processing and sufficiency: the type of an i.i.d. message is a
    sufficient statistic (zero parse defect), a lossy parse is not.
 9. Rissanen rates: capacity of Bernoulli families vs log2(n+1), and the
    explicit Chebyshev packing lower bound (15/32) log2 n - 8.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[Vector]  # p[theta][x]

LOG2 = math.log(2.0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic information-theoretic quantities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Shannon entropy H(p) in bits, with the convention 0 log 0 = 0."""
    return -sum(pi * math.log2(pi) for pi in p if pi > 0.0)


def min_entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Min-entropy H_inf(p) = -log2 max_x p(x), in bits."""
    return -math.log2(max(p))


def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Relative entropy D(p || q) in bits.  Requires q(x) > 0 wherever p(x) > 0."""
    total = 0.0
    for pi, qi in zip(p, q):
        if pi > 0.0:
            total += pi * math.log2(pi / qi)
    return total


def chi_squared(a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """chi^2(a || b) = sum_x (a(x) - b(x))^2 / b(x)."""
    return sum((ai - bi) ** 2 / bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b))


def mixture(weights: Sequence[float], sources: Matrix) -> Vector:
    """The Bayes mixture m_w(x) = sum_theta w_theta p_theta(x)."""
    n = len(sources[0])
    return [sum(w * p[x] for w, p in zip(weights, sources)) for x in range(n)]


def mutual_info_bits(weights: Sequence[float], sources: Matrix) -> float:
    """I(w) = sum_theta w_theta D(p_theta || m_w)."""
    m = mixture(weights, sources)
    return sum(w * kl_bits(p, m) for w, p in zip(weights, sources) if w > 0.0)


def shtarkov_sum(sources: Matrix) -> float:
    """C_S = sum_x max_theta p_theta(x); log2 C_S is the worst-case price."""
    n = len(sources[0])
    return sum(max(p[x] for p in sources) for x in range(n))


def nml(sources: Matrix) -> Vector:
    """Normalized maximum-likelihood distribution (the worst-case optimum)."""
    cs = shtarkov_sum(sources)
    n = len(sources[0])
    return [max(p[x] for p in sources) / cs for x in range(n)]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Blahut-Arimoto: compute the capacity with a certified bracket
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def blahut_arimoto(
    sources: Matrix,
    iterations: int = 4000,
    tol: float = 1e-13,
    prior0: Sequence[float] | None = None,
) -> Tuple[float, Vector, Vector, float, float]:
    """Compute the capacity C of a source class by alternating maximisation.

    Returns (C_estimate, optimal_prior, optimal_mixture, lower_cert, upper_cert),
    where lower_cert = I(w) <= C <= upper_cert = max_theta D(p_theta || m_w).
    The bracket is rigorous at every iteration: the lower certificate holds by
    definition of C as a supremum, and the upper certificate by the verification
    criterion (any coding distribution within c bits of every source forces C <= c).
    """
    k = len(sources)
    w = list(prior0) if prior0 is not None else [1.0 / k] * k
    m = mixture(w, sources)
    lower = mutual_info_bits(w, sources)
    upper = max(kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources)
    for _ in range(iterations):
        m = mixture(w, sources)
        d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
        lower = sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d))
        upper = max(d)
        new = [wi * (2.0 ** di) for wi, di in zip(w, d)]
        z = sum(new)
        w = [v / z for v in new]
        if upper - lower < tol:
            break
    m = mixture(w, sources)
    d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
    lower = sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d))
    upper = max(d)
    return 0.5 * (lower + upper), w, m, lower, upper


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Source-class constructors
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def shift_class(p0: Sequence[float]) -> Matrix:
    """Unknown-offset class over Z/|A|:  p_theta(x) = p0(x - theta)."""
    n = len(p0)
    return [[p0[(x - theta) % n] for x in range(n)] for theta in range(n)]


def iid_binary_class(n: int, params: Sequence[float]) -> Matrix:
    """The i.i.d. Bernoulli(t) laws on {0,1}^n, messages indexed by 0..2^n-1."""
    out: Matrix = []
    for t in params:
        row: Vector = []
        for code in range(2 ** n):
            ones = bin(code).count("1")
            row.append((t ** ones) * ((1.0 - t) ** (n - ones)))
        out.append(row)
    return out


def log_binom(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    return math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(n - k + 1)


def binomial_law(n: int, t: float) -> Vector:
    """Law of the number of ones -- the sufficient statistic of Bernoulli(t) on n bits."""
    return [math.exp(log_binom(n, k) + k * math.log(t) + (n - k) * math.log1p(-t))
            for k in range(n + 1)]


def tensor_class(s: Matrix, t: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """The product class: independent blocks, parameters range over pairs."""
    out: Matrix = []
    for ps in s:
        for pt in t:
            out.append([a * b for a in ps for b in pt])
    return out


def smooth_class(sources: Matrix, eps: float) -> Matrix:
    """eps-smoothing: (1-eps) p_theta + eps * uniform, making the class positive."""
    n = len(sources[0])
    return [[(1.0 - eps) * pi + eps / n for pi in p] for p in sources]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parses: pushforward, chain rule and the parse defect
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pushforward(f: Callable[[int], int], p: Sequence[float], n_out: int) -> Vector:
    """(f_* p)(y) = sum_{x : f(x)=y} p(x)."""
    out = [0.0] * n_out
    for x, px in enumerate(p):
        out[f(x)] += px
    return out


def parse_defect(
    f: Callable[[int], int], p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float], n_out: int
) -> float:
    """The within-fibre defect D(p || q | f) = D(p||q) - D(f_*p || f_*q).

    By the chain rule this equals the divergence between the conditional laws of
    p and q inside the fibres of f, so it is >= 0, and it vanishes exactly when f
    is a sufficient statistic (Fisher-Neyman factorisation).
    """
    fp = pushforward(f, p, n_out)
    fq = pushforward(f, q, n_out)
    return kl_bits(p, q) - kl_bits(fp, fq)

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[Vector]


def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(pi * math.log2(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0.0)


def mixture(w: Sequence[float], sources: Matrix) -> Vector:
    n = len(sources[0])
    return [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(n)]


def blahut_arimoto(sources: Matrix, prior0: Sequence[float] | None = None,
                   iters: int = 8000) -> Tuple[float, Vector, Vector, Vector]:
    k = len(sources)
    w: Vector = list(prior0) if prior0 else [1.0 / k] * k
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = mixture(w, sources)
        d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
        if max(d) - sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) < 1e-13:
            break
        scaled = [wi * 2.0 ** di for wi, di in zip(w, d)]
        z = sum(scaled)
        w = [v / z for v in scaled]
    m = mixture(w, sources)
    d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
    cap = 0.5 * (sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) + max(d))
    return cap, w, m, d


def main() -> None:
    sources: Matrix = [[0.70, 0.20, 0.10], [0.10, 0.70, 0.20], [0.25, 0.25, 0.50]]
    cap, w, m, d = blahut_arimoto(sources)

    print(f"capacity C          = {cap:.10f} bits per message")
    print("optimal prior w*    =", [round(x, 6) for x in w])
    print("optimal code m*     =", [round(x, 6) for x in m])
    print()
    print("saddle point / equalizer:")
    for i, di in enumerate(d):
        tag = "= C (in support)" if w[i] > 1e-6 else "<= C (weight 0)"
        print(f"   D(p_{i} || m*) = {di:.10f}   {tag}")
    print()

    # no coding distribution does better: scan a fine grid of the simplex
    best, arg = float("inf"), None
    steps = 120
    for i in range(1, steps):
        for j in range(1, steps - i):
            q = [i / steps, j / steps, 1 - i / steps - j / steps]
            val = max(kl_bits(p, q) for p in sources)

import math
from typing import List, Sequence

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[Vector]


def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(pi * math.log2(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0.0)


def entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return -sum(x * math.log2(x) for x in p if x > 0.0)


def min_entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return -math.log2(max(p))


def capacity(sources: Matrix, iters: int = 8000) -> float:
    k, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    w: Vector = [1.0 / k] * k
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(n)]
        d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
        if max(d) - sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) < 1e-13:

        w = [v / z for v in scaled]
    m = [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(n)]
    d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
    return 0.5 * (sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) + max(d))


def shtarkov_sum(sources: Matrix) -> float:
    return sum(max(p[x] for p in sources) for x in range(len(sources[0])))


def shift_class(p0: Sequence[float]) -> Matrix:
    n = len(p0)
    return [[p0[(x - t) % n] for x in range(n)] for t in range(n)]


def tensor(s: Matrix, t: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[a * b for a in ps for b in pt] for ps in s for pt in t]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Sequence

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[Vector]


def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(pi * math.log2(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 1e-300)


def log_binom(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    return math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(n - k + 1)


def binomial_law(n: int, t: float) -> Vector:
    """Distribution of the number of ones -- the sufficient statistic of Bernoulli(t)."""
    return [math.exp(log_binom(n, k) + k * math.log(t) + (n - k) * math.log1p(-t))
            for k in range(n + 1)]


def capacity(sources: Matrix, iters: int = 3000) -> float:
    k, n = len(sources), len(sources[0])
    w: Vector = [1.0 / k] * k
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(n)]
        d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
        if max(d) - sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) < 1e-12:

        z = sum(scaled)

    d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
    return 0.5 * (sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) + max(d))

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]

def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(pi * math.log2(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0.0)


def pushforward(f: Callable[[int], int], p: Sequence[float], n_out: int) -> Vector:
    """(f_* p)(y) = sum over the fibre of y."""
    out = [0.0] * n_out
    for x, px in enumerate(p):
        out[f(x)] += px
    return out


def within_fibre_defect(
    f: Callable[[int], int], p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float], n_out: int
) -> float:
    """D(p || q | f), computed directly from the conditional laws in each fibre."""
    fp = pushforward(f, p, n_out)
    fq = pushforward(f, q, n_out)
    total = 0.0
    for x, px in enumerate(p):
        if px <= 0.0:
            continue
        y = f(x)
        cond_p = px / fp[y]
        cond_q = q[x] / fq[y]
        total += px * math.log2(cond_p / cond_q)
    return total

    coding: Sequence[float],

def log_binom(n: int, k: int) -> float:
    return math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(n - k + 1)


def window_mass(n: int, t: float, lo: float, hi: float) -> float:
    """Exact probability that the number of ones lies in the open interval (lo, hi)."""
    total = 0.0
    k_lo = max(0, math.ceil(lo))
    k_hi = min(n, math.floor(hi))
    for k in range(k_lo, k_hi + 1):
        total += math.exp(log_binom(n, k) + k * math.log(t) + (n - k) * math.log1p(-t))
    return total

    """Verify the packing at message length n and return the certified lower bound."""
    k = math.isqrt(n)

    half = 2.0 * n / k
    biases = [(4 * j + 2) / k for j in range(count)]
    means = [n * t for t in biases]
    windows: List[Tuple[float, float]] = [(mu - half, mu + half) for mu in means]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return -sum(x * math.log2(x) for x in p if x > 0)


def min_entropy_bits(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return -math.log2(max(p))


def kl_bits(p: Sequence[float], q: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return sum(pi * math.log2(pi / qi) for pi, qi in zip(p, q) if pi > 0)


def shift_class(p0: Sequence[float]) -> List[List[float]]:
    n = len(p0)
    return [[p0[(x - t) % n] for x in range(n)] for t in range(n)]


def capacity(sources: List[List[float]], iters: int = 3000) -> float:
    k = len(sources)
    w = [1.0 / k] * k
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(len(sources[0]))]
        d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
        lo, hi = sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)), max(d)
        if hi - lo < 1e-13:
            break
        nw = [wi * 2.0 ** di for wi, di in zip(w, d)]
        z = sum(nw)
        w = [v / z for v in nw]
    m = [sum(wi * p[x] for wi, p in zip(w, sources)) for x in range(len(sources[0]))]
    d = [kl_bits(p, m) for p in sources]
    return 0.5 * (sum(wi * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)) + max(d))

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def kl_bits(p: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray) -> float:
    mask = p > 0
    return float(np.sum(p[mask] * np.log2(p[mask] / np.maximum(q[mask], 1e-300))))


def binom_pmf(n: int, t: float) -> np.ndarray:
    ks = np.arange(n + 1)
    log_pmf = (
        np.array([math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(n - k + 1) for k in ks])
        + ks * math.log(max(t, 1e-300))
        + (n - ks) * math.log(max(1 - t, 1e-300))
    )
    return np.exp(log_pmf)


def capacity(rows: List[np.ndarray], iters: int = 2500) -> float:
    k = len(rows)
    w = np.full(k, 1.0 / k)
    for _ in range(iters):
        m = np.tensordot(w, np.array(rows), axes=1)
        d = np.array([kl_bits(r, m) for r in rows])
        lo, hi = float(w @ d), float(d.max())
        if hi - lo < 1e-12:
            break
        w = w * np.exp2(d)
        w /= w.sum()
    m = np.tensordot(w, np.array(rows), axes=1)
    d = np.array([kl_bits(r, m) for r in rows])
    return 0.5 * (float(w @ d) + float(d.max()))


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.2, 5.2))

    # --- left: capacity growth --------------------------------------------------
    ns = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]
    caps = []
    for n in ns:
        K = 32
        rows = [binom_pmf(n, (2 * j + 1) / (2 * K)) for j in range(K)]

    ax2.set_ylabel("probability")

  let w = v.map(x=>Math.max(x,EPS)); const s=w.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
  return w.map(x=>x/s);
}
function kl(p,q){let t=0;for(let i=0;i<p.length;i++){if(p[i]>0)t+=p[i]*Math.log2(p[i]/q[i]);}return t;}
function H(p){let t=0;for(const x of p) if(x>0) t-=x*Math.log2(x); return t;}
function mix(w,S){const n=S[0].length;const m=new Array(n).fill(0);
  for(let k=0;k<S.length;k++) for(let i=0;i<n;i++) m[i]+=w[k]*S[k][i]; return m;}
function blahut(S,iters=3000){
  let w = new Array(S.length).fill(1/S.length), lo=0, hi=0, m=mix(w,S);
  for(let s=0;s<iters;s++){
    m = mix(w,S);
    const d = S.map(p=>kl(p,m));
    lo = w.reduce((a,wi,i)=>a+wi*d[i],0); hi = Math.max(...d);
    if(hi-lo < 1e-13) break;
    const nw = w.map((wi,i)=>wi*Math.pow(2,d[i]));
    const z = nw.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
    w = nw.map(v=>v/z);
  }
  m = mix(w,S);
  const d = S.map(p=>kl(p,m));
  lo = w.reduce((a,wi,i)=>a+wi*d[i],0); hi = Math.max(...d);
  return {w,m,d,lo,hi,C:0.5*(lo+hi)};
}
function shtarkov(S){const n=S[0].length;let t=0;
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++) t+=Math.max(...S.map(p=>p[i])); return t;}
function nmlOf(S){const cs=shtarkov(S);const n=S[0].length;
  const out=[];for(let i=0;i<n;i++) out.push(Math.max(...S.map(p=>p[i]))/cs); return out;}

// ---- sliders (two per source: p(a) and p(b) as fractions of what remains) ----
const holder = document.getElementById('sliders');
const state = S.map(p=>p.slice());
function buildSliders(){
  holder.innerHTML='';
  state.forEach((p,k)=>{
    [0,1].forEach(j=>{
      const row=document.createElement('div'); row.className='srcrow';
      const lab=document.createElement('label');
      lab.innerHTML = 'src '+k+'   p('+['a','b'][j]+')';
      const inp=document.createElement('input');

      inp.value = Math.round(p[j]*100);

      val.textContent = p[j].toFixed(2);
      inp.addEventListener('input',()=>{
        let a = (+document.querySelectorAll('.srcrow input')[2*k].value)/100;
        let b = (+document.querySelectorAll('.srcrow input')[2*k+1].value)/100;
        if(a+b>0.99){const s=0.99/(a+b); a*=s; b*=s;}
        state[k]=clampSimplex([a,b,1-a-b]);
        document.querySelectorAll('.srcrow .val')[2*k].textContent=state[k][0].toFixed(2);
        document.querySelectorAll('.srcrow .val')[2*k+1].textContent=state[k][1].toFixed(2);

}
document.querySelectorAll('.presets button').forEach(b=>{
  b.addEventListener('click',()=>{
    const P=PRESETS[b.dataset.p];

// ---- simplex drawing ----
const cv=document.getElementById('cv'), ctx=cv.getContext('2d');
const V=[[310,40],[40,500],[580,500]];  // a, b, c corners
function toXY(p){return [p[0]*V[0][0]+p[1]*V[1][0]+p[2]*V[2][0],
                         p[0]*V[0][1]+p[1]*V[1][1]+p[2]*V[2][1]];}
function drawSimplex(res){
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,cv.width,cv.height);
  // divergence heat map towards m*
  const img=ctx.createImageData(cv.width,cv.height);
  const m=res.m, C=res.C;
  for(let y=0;y<cv.height;y+=1){
    for(let x=0;x<cv.width;x+=1){
      const l = bary(x,y);
      const idx=4*(y*cv.width+x);
      if(l && l[0]>=0&&l[1]>=0&&l[2]>=0){
        const p=clampSimplex(l);
        const d=kl(p,m);
        const t=Math.min(1,d/Math.max(C,1e-6));
        img.data[idx]  = 12+70*t;
        img.data[idx+1]= 18+40*t;
        img.data[idx+2]= 32+90*t;
        img.data[idx+3]= 255;
      } else { img.data[idx+3]=0; }
    }
  }
  ctx.putImageData(img,0,0);
  ctx.strokeStyle='#3a465c'; ctx.lineWidth=1.5;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(...V[0]); ctx.lineTo(...V[1]); ctx.lineTo(...V[2]); ctx.closePath(); ctx.stroke();
  ctx.fillStyle='#93a1b8'; ctx.font='13px system-ui';
  ctx.fillText('a',V[0][0]-4,V[0][1]-12); ctx.fillText('b',V[1][0]-10,V[1][1]+18);
  ctx.fillText('c',V[2][0]+4,V[2][1]+18);
  // nml
  const nm=nmlOf(state), nxy=toXY(nm);
  ctx.strokeStyle='#5ddc9b'; ctx.lineWidth=2;
  ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(nxy[0],nxy[1],7,0,6.2832); ctx.stroke();
  // sources
  state.forEach((p,k)=>{
    const [x,y]=toXY(p);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x,y,5.5,0,6.2832); ctx.fillStyle='#6ea8fe'; ctx.fill();
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x,y,7+18*res.w[k],0,6.2832);
    ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(110,168,254,.55)'; ctx.lineWidth=1.5; ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle='#93a1b8'; ctx.font='12px system-ui'; ctx.fillText('p'+k,x+11,y-9);
  });
  // mixture
  const [mx,my]=toXY(res.m);
  star(mx,my,9,'#ff9f68');
}
function star(cx,cy,r,color){
  ctx.beginPath();
  for(let i=0;i<10;i++){
    const ang=-Math.PI/2+i*Math.PI/5, rr=(i%2===0)?r:r*0.45;
    const x=cx+rr*Math.cos(ang), y=cy+rr*Math.sin(ang);
    i?ctx.lineTo(x,y):ctx.moveTo(x,y);
  }
  ctx.closePath(); ctx.fillStyle=color; ctx.fill();
}
function bary(x,y){
  const [x1,y1]=V[0],[x2,y2]=V[1],[x3,y3]=V[2];
  const det=(y2-y3)*(x1-x3)+(x3-x2)*(y1-y3);
  const l1=((y2-y3)*(x-x3)+(x3-x2)*(y-y3))/det;
  const l2=((y3-y1)*(x-x3)+(x1-x3)*(y-y3))/det;
  return [l1,l2,1-l1-l2];
}

function render(){
  const res=blahut(state);
  const C=res.C, worst=Math.log2(shtarkov(state)), twopart=Math.log2(3);
  document.getElementById('cap').innerHTML=C.toFixed(6)+'<span class="unit">bits / message</span>';
  document.getElementById('bracket').textContent =
    'certified enclosure: ['+res.lo.toFixed(9)+', '+res.hi.toFixed(9)+']';

  document.getElementById('avg').textContent=C.toFixed(5);

  document.getElementById('bworst').style.width=(100*worst/scale)+'%';
  document.getElementById('bavg').style.width=(100*C/scale)+'%';
  document.getElementById('btp').style.width=(100*twopart/scale)+'%';
  document.getElementById('ordering').innerHTML =
    'C = '+C.toFixed(5)+' ≤ log₂ Cₛ = '+worst.toFixed(5)+
    ' ≤ ... and C ≤ log₂|Θ| = '+twopart.toFixed(5)+
    '.  The average-case price never exceeds the worst-case price; the gap here is '+
    (worst-C).toFixed(5)+' bits.';

  // equalizer bars
  const eq=document.getElementById('eq'); eq.innerHTML='';
  const dmax=Math.max(...res.d,C)*1.15+1e-9;
  res.d.forEach((d,k)=>{
    const lbl=document.createElement('div'); lbl.className='lbl';
    lbl.innerHTML='<span>source '+k+(res.w[k]>1e-4?' (in support)':' (weight 0)')+
      '</span><span>'+d.toFixed(6)+'</span>';
    const bar=document.createElement('div'); bar.className='bar';
    const fill=document.createElement('div'); fill.style.width=(100*d/dmax)+'%';
    if(res.w[k]<=1e-4) fill.style.background='linear-gradient(90deg,#4b5566,#6b7688)';
    bar.appendChild(fill); eq.appendChild(lbl); eq.appendChild(bar);
  });
  const capline=document.createElement('div');
  capline.className='note';
  capline.innerHTML='dashed capacity level: <strong>'+C.toFixed(6)+'</strong> bits — '+
    'every bar in the support of the optimal prior sits exactly on it.';
  eq.appendChild(capline);

  const tb=document.querySelector('#wtable tbody'); tb.innerHTML='';
  res.w.forEach((wi,k)=>{
    const tr=document.createElement('tr');
    tr.innerHTML='<td>p'+k+'</td><td>'+wi.toFixed(6)+'</td><td>'+res.d[k].toFixed(6)+'</td>';
    tb.appendChild(tr);
  });

  const pt=document.querySelector('#ptable tbody'); pt.innerHTML='';
  state.forEach((p,k)=>{
    const tr=document.createElement('tr');
    tr.innerHTML='<td>p'+k+'</td>'+p.map(v=>'<td>'+v.toFixed(3)+'</td>').join('')+
                 '<td>'+H(p).toFixed(4)+'</td>';
    pt.appendChild(tr);
  });

  const eqOK = res.w.every((wi,k)=> wi<=1e-4 || Math.abs(res.d[k]-C)<1e-6);
  const satOK = res.d.every(d=>d<=C+1e-6);
  const posOK = C>1e-9;
  document.getElementById('flags').innerHTML =
    '<span class="pill '+(satOK?'ok':'')+'">saddle point: D ≤ C for all sources</span>'+
    '<span class="pill '+(eqOK?'ok':'')+'">equalizer on the support</span>'+
    '<span class="pill '+(posOK?'ok':'')+'">price > 0 unless the class is a point</span>';

  drawSimplex(res);
}
buildSliders(); render();
</script>

    {
      "title": "The Rissanen Bracket — How the Price Grows with Message Length",
      "description": "A live exploration of the logarithmic growth of the price of universality for the binary memoryless class. Sliding the message length and the number of parameters recomputes the exact capacity on the sufficient statistic (the count of ones) using a numerically stable binomial law, and plots it against the proved upper bound log2(n+1), the classical rate (1/2) log2 n and the proved lower bound (15/32) log2 n - 8 on a logarithmic axis. A second canvas draws the Chebyshev packing that forces the lower bound: the count distributions of the packed biases at scale k = floor(sqrt n), with their shaded windows of half-width 2n/k visibly disjoint, alongside a table reporting the scale, the number of packed sources, the spacing of the means, the Chebyshev tail bound and the guaranteed window mass.",

<html lang="en">
<head>

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Rissanen Bracket</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    A universal coder facing all Bernoulli sources on $n$-bit messages pays a price that
    grows like $\tfrac12\log_2 n$ bits — not per bit, in total. Slide $n$ and watch the
    exact capacity of the family sit inside its proved bracket, and see the packing of
    distinguishable parameters that forces the lower bound.
  </p>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>Controls</h2>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>message length $n$</label>
      <input id="n" type="range" min="4" max="4096" step="1" value="256">
      <div class="v" id="nv">256</div>
    </div>
    <div class="ctl">
      <label>parameters in the family</label>
      <input id="k" type="range" min="2" max="64" step="1" value="24">
      <div class="v" id="kv">24</div>
    </div>
    <div style="margin-top:14px">
      <div class="stat"><b id="cap">—</b><span>capacity $C$ (bits)</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><b id="half">—</b><span>$\tfrac12\log_2 n$</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><b id="up">—</b><span>upper bound $\log_2(n+1)$</span></div>
      <div class="stat"><b id="low">—</b><span>lower bound $\tfrac{15}{32}\log_2 n-8$</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>Capacity versus message length</h2>
    <canvas id="plot" width="960" height="420"></canvas>
    <div class="legend" style="margin-top:10px">
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#6ea8fe"></i>capacity of the family (computed)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#ff9f68"></i>$\tfrac12\log_2 n$ (classical rate)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#5ddc9b"></i>$\log_2(n+1)$ (proved upper bound)</span>
      <span><i class="swatch" style="background:#f7d070"></i>$\tfrac{15}{32}\log_2 n-8$ (proved lower bound)</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>The packing that forces the lower bound</h2>
    <canvas id="pack" width="960" height="300"></canvas>
    <div class="legend" style="margin-top:10px">
      <span>Each curve is the distribution of the number of ones under one packed
      parameter $t_j=(4j+2)/k$, $k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. Shaded bands are the
      Chebyshev windows of half-width $2n/k$: pairwise disjoint, each carrying at least
      $15/16$ of its source's mass.</span>
    </div>
    <table style="margin-top:12px">
      <thead><tr><th>quantity</th><th>value</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody id="ptab"></tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <details>
    <summary>Click to reveal: why $\log_2 n$, and why the constant is between $15/32$ and $1$</summary>
    <div class="body">
      <p><strong>Upper bound.</strong> For an i.i.d. family, the number of ones is a
      <em>sufficient statistic</em>: the probability of a message depends on it alone.
      A parse that is a sufficient statistic costs nothing, so the price of the family
      equals the price of coding the count — and the count lives in a space of $n+1$
      points, whose price is at most $\log_2(n+1)$ by the two-part bound. Note that this
      holds no matter how many parameters the family contains.</p>
      <p><strong>Lower bound.</strong> Choose the parameters $t_j=(4j+2)/k$ with
      $k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. Under $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(t_j)$ the count has mean $nt_j$
      and variance $nt_j(1-t_j)\le n/4$, so by Chebyshev at least a fraction $15/16$ of its
      mass lies within $2n/k$ of the mean. Consecutive means are $4n/k$ apart, so the
      windows are disjoint: the $\lfloor k/4\rfloor$ sources are approximately
      distinguishable. A class of $N$ distinguishable sources costs at least
      $(1-\delta)\log_2 N-4$, which with $N=\lfloor k/4\rfloor\ge\sqrt n/8$ and
      $\delta=1/16$ gives $\tfrac{15}{32}\log_2 n-8$.</p>
      <p>The residual gap between $15/32$ and the classical $1/2$ is exactly the
      Chebyshev tail factor $15/16$; a sharper tail estimate would close it.</p>
    </div>
  </details>

<script>
function lgamma(x){ // Lanczos
  const g=7,c=[0.99999999999980993,676.5203681218851,-1259.1392167224028,
    771.32342877765313,-176.61502916214059,12.507343278686905,
    -0.13857109526572012,9.9843695780195716e-6,1.5056327351493116e-7];
  if(x<0.5) return Math.log(Math.PI/Math.sin(Math.PI*x))-lgamma(1-x);
  x-=1; let a=c[0]; const t=x+g+0.5;
  for(let i=1;i<g+2;i++) a+=c[i]/(x+i);
  return 0.5*Math.log(2*Math.PI)+(x+0.5)*Math.log(t)-t+Math.log(a);
}
function logChoose(n,k){return lgamma(n+1)-lgamma(k+1)-lgamma(n-k+1);}
function binomPMF(n,t){
  const out=new Float64Array(n+1);
  const lt=Math.log(Math.max(t,1e-300)), l1t=Math.log(Math.max(1-t,1e-300));
  for(let i=0;i<=n;i++) out[i]=Math.exp(logChoose(n,i)+i*lt+(n-i)*l1t);
  return out;
}
function klRows(p,m){let s=0;for(let i=0;i<p.length;i++){const pi=p[i];
  if(pi>1e-300) s+=pi*Math.log2(pi/Math.max(m[i],1e-300));} return s;}
function capacityOf(rows,iters=300){
  const K=rows.length,n=rows[0].length;
  let w=new Float64Array(K).fill(1/K), lo=0, hi=0;
  const m=new Float64Array(n);
  for(let s=0;s<iters;s++){
    m.fill(0);
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){const wk=w[k]; if(wk>0){const r=rows[k];
      for(let i=0;i<n;i++) m[i]+=wk*r[i];}}
    const d=new Float64Array(K); let z=0;
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++) d[k]=klRows(rows[k],m);
    lo=0; hi=-1e18;
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){lo+=w[k]*d[k]; if(d[k]>hi)hi=d[k];}
    if(hi-lo<1e-11) break;
    const nw=new Float64Array(K);
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++){nw[k]=w[k]*Math.pow(2,d[k]); z+=nw[k];}
    for(let k=0;k<K;k++) w[k]=nw[k]/z;
  }
  return {C:0.5*(lo+hi),lo:lo,hi:hi,w:w};
}
function familyRows(n,K){
  const rows=[];
  for(let j=0;j<K;j++){const t=(2*j+1)/(2*K); rows.push(binomPMF(n,t));}
  return rows;
}

const nEl=document.getElementById('n'), kEl=document.getElementById('k');
const plot=document.getElementById('plot'), pc=plot.getContext('2d');
const pack=document.getElementById('pack'), qc=pack.getContext('2d');
let cache={};

function capAt(n,K){
  const key=n+'/'+K;
  if(cache[key]!==undefined) return cache[key];
  const v=capacityOf(familyRows(n,K)).C; cache[key]=v; return v;
}

function drawPlot(nSel,K){
  const W=plot.width,Hh=plot.height,L=62,R=18,T=18,B=42;
  pc.clearRect(0,0,W,Hh);
  const ns=[]; for(let e=2;e<=12.02;e+=0.5) ns.push(Math.round(Math.pow(2,e)));
  const xs=n=>L+(Math.log2(n)-2)/(12-2)*(W-L-R);
  const ymax=13, ys=v=>Hh-B-(Math.max(v,-9)+9)/(ymax+9)*(Hh-T-B);
  // grid
  pc.strokeStyle='#222a38'; pc.fillStyle='#93a1b8'; pc.font='11px system-ui'; pc.lineWidth=1;
  for(let e=2;e<=12;e+=1){
    const x=xs(Math.pow(2,e));
    pc.beginPath(); pc.moveTo(x,T); pc.lineTo(x,Hh-B); pc.stroke();
    pc.fillText('2^'+e,x-9,Hh-B+16);
  }
  for(let v=-8;v<=12;v+=4){
    const y=ys(v);
    pc.beginPath(); pc.moveTo(L,y); pc.lineTo(W-R,y); pc.stroke();
    pc.fillText(String(v),L-26,y+4);
  }
  pc.fillText('message length n (log scale)',W/2-80,Hh-6);
  pc.save(); pc.translate(16,Hh/2); pc.rotate(-Math.PI/2);
  pc.fillText('bits',0,0); pc.restore();
  const curve=(f,color,dash)=>{
    pc.strokeStyle=color; pc.lineWidth=2; pc.setLineDash(dash||[]);
    pc.beginPath();
    ns.forEach((n,i)=>{const x=xs(n),y=ys(f(n)); i?pc.lineTo(x,y):pc.moveTo(x,y);});
    pc.stroke(); pc.setLineDash([]);
  };
  curve(n=>Math.log2(n+1),'#5ddc9b');
  curve(n=>0.5*Math.log2(n),'#ff9f68',[6,4]);
  curve(n=>(15/32)*Math.log2(n)-8,'#f7d070');
  // computed capacity (coarser grid, it is the expensive one)
  const cs=[]; for(let e=2;e<=12.02;e+=1) cs.push(Math.round(Math.pow(2,e)));
  pc.strokeStyle='#6ea8fe'; pc.lineWidth=2.5; pc.beginPath();
  cs.forEach((n,i)=>{const x=xs(n),y=ys(capAt(n,K)); i?pc.lineTo(x,y):pc.moveTo(x,y);});

  "interactive_layout": "# The Price of Universality

### One decompressor must serve everybody. What does that cost, exactly?

Every compressed file arrives with an invisible companion: the program that knows how
to read it. That program is *shared* — the same decompressor serves your photos, your
source code, your genome. A decompressor specialised to one kind of data would produce
shorter files. The question this page answers is: **how much shorter, exactly?**

The answer is startlingly clean. The waste is not a vague engineering quantity; it is
an exact number attached to the family of data sources you care about, and it is a
number information theorists already know from a completely different context: the
**capacity of a communication channel**.

---

## 1. Warm-up: a probability distribution *is* a code

Fix a finite set $X$ of possible messages. A *source* is a probability distribution $p$
on $X$. If your compressor believes message $x$ has probability $q(x)$, the best it can
do is spend about

$$\ell(x) = \log_2\frac{1}{q(x)}\ \text{ bits on } x .$$

Likely messages get short codewords; unlikely ones get long ones. So "designing a
decompressor" and "choosing a probability distribution $q$ on messages" are the same
activity. We call $q$ the **coding distribution**.

If the data really comes from $p$ but your decompressor believes $q$, the bits you
waste per message are the **relative entropy**

$$D(p\,\|\,q)=\sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\ \ge\ 0,$$

zero exactly when $q=p$. This is the currency in which the price of universality is
paid.

<details>
<summary><strong>Why is $\log_2(1/q(x))$ really the best you can do?</strong> (click to expand)</summary>

A binary prefix-free code with codeword lengths $\ell(x)$ exists if and only if it
satisfies the Kraft inequality $\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)}\le 1$. Setting $q(x)=2^{-\ell(x)}$
turns any such code into a sub-probability distribution, and conversely rounding
$\lceil\log_2(1/q(x))\rceil$ turns any distribution into a code losing less than one
bit. Averaging, the expected length of the code built from $q$ is

$$\sum_x p(x)\,\ell(x)\;=\;H(p)+D(p\|q)\;(+\,\text{at most }1),$$

where $H(p)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)$ is the entropy. The entropy is what a
decompressor that *knew* $p$ would spend; $D(p\|q)$ is the surcharge for believing
something else. Everything on this page is about that surcharge. See
[Kraft's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraft%E2%80%93McMillan_inequality)
and [relative entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence)
for background.

</details>

---

## 2. The minimax question, and the theorem that answers it

A universal scheme faces not one source but a whole family $\{p_\theta\}_{\theta\in\Theta}$.
It must commit to a single $q$ before seeing which $\theta$ nature picked. So the price
of universality is

$$R^\star=\min_{q}\ \max_{\theta}\ D(p_\theta\,\|\,q).$$

Saddle-point problems are usually opaque. This one is not.

> **Redundancy–Capacity Theorem.** For a finite family of strictly positive sources on
> a finite message space,
> $$\min_{q}\max_{\theta} D(p_\theta\|q)\;=\;C\;:=\;\max_{w}\sum_\theta w_\theta\,
> D\!\Big(p_\theta\,\Big\|\,\textstyle\sum_{\theta'}w_{\theta'}p_{\theta'}\Big),$$
> the maximum over all priors $w$ on the parameter set. The maximum is attained; the
> optimal $q$ is the mixture $m_{w^\star}$ over a maximising prior; and no coding
> distribution beats $C$ against every source at once.

Write $m_w=\sum_\theta w_\theta p_\theta$ for the **Bayes mixture**. The inner quantity
is exactly the **mutual information** between the identity of the source and the message
it emits:

$$I(w)=\sum_\theta w_\theta D(p_\theta\|m_w)=H(m_w)-\sum_\theta w_\theta H(p_\theta).$$

So here is the punchline in plain English:

> **The bits a universal decompressor wastes are exactly the bits the data leaks about
> its own identity.**

If all your sources look alike, the message tells you nothing about which one produced
it, the channel has no capacity, and universality is free. If a genome never looks like
a JPEG, the message screams its provenance — and you pay for it.

---

## 4. Why the theorem is true: a nudge and a quadratic

Classical proofs invoke a minimax theorem. There is a more elementary and more
revealing route, and it is worth seeing because it explains *why* an average-optimal
code turns out to be uniformly optimal.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the proof</strong></summary>

Start from an identity that is pure algebra — the **compensation identity**. For any
prior $w$ and any coding distribution $q$,

$$\sum_\theta w_\theta D(p_\theta\|q)\;=\;I(w)\;+\;D(m_w\|q).$$

Take a prior $w^\star$ maximising $I$; one exists because $I$ is continuous (visible
from the entropy formula) on the compact simplex of priors. Pick a single source
$\theta_0$ and nudge the prior towards it,

$$w_t=(1-t)w^\star+t\,\delta_{\theta_0},\qquad 0<t\le1 .$$

Apply the compensation identity to $w_t$ using the *old* mixture $m^\star$ as the
coding distribution. The left side is $(1-t)I(w^\star)+t\,D(p_{\theta_0}\|m^\star)$;
the right side is $I(w_t)+D(m_{w_t}\|m^\star)$ with $I(w_t)\le I(w^\star)$. Hence

$$t\big(D(p_{\theta_0}\|m^\star)-C\big)\;\le\;D(m_{w_t}\|m^\star).$$

Now the nudged mixture differs from the old one by exactly
$m_{w_t}-m^\star=t\,(p_{\theta_0}-m^\star)$, and relative entropy is dominated by the
chi-squared distance,

$$D(a\|b)\le\frac1{\ln2}\sum_x\frac{(a(x)-b(x))^2}{b(x)},$$

so the right-hand side is $O(t^2)$. Divide by $t$, let $t\to0$: the first-order term
must be non-positive, i.e. $D(p_{\theta_0}\|m^\star)\le C$ for **every** $\theta_0$.

That is the whole theorem: a derivative computation in disguise, carried out with an
inequality instead of a derivative. Two bonuses fall out immediately. Any source with
positive prior weight pays *exactly* $C$ (the equalizer property), and two different
capacity-achieving priors always induce the *same* mixture — so the best universal
decompressor is a canonical object attached to the family, not an artefact of the
optimisation.

</details>

The algorithm that computes all of this is the Blahut–Arimoto iteration. It has a lovely
feature the saddle point hands us for free: it returns a **certified bracket** around
the capacity at every step, not just an estimate.

## 5. Two prices, and the exact gap between them

There is an older, harsher way to measure universality: demand a guarantee for *every
individual message*, not on average. That minimax is also exactly solved, by the
**Shtarkov sum** $C_S=\sum_x\max_\theta p_\theta(x)$, whose logarithm is the worst-case
price. The two are ordered, $C\le\log_2 C_S$ — but they are genuinely different numbers.

Consider an **unknown-offset class**: a base law $p_0$ on a finite abelian group $A$,
translated by an unknown group element, $p_\theta(x)=p_0(x-\theta)$ (a known waveform at
unknown phase; a known histogram at unknown cyclic shift). Symmetry computes both prices
in closed form:

$$C=\log_2|A|-H(p_0),\qquad \log_2 C_S=\log_2|A|-H_\infty(p_0),$$

where $H_\infty(p_0)=-\log_2\max_a p_0(a)$ is the
[min-entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Min-entropy). Therefore

> **worst case $-$ average case $=H(p_0)-H_\infty(p_0)$**, exactly the gap between
> Shannon entropy and min-entropy.

The smallest interesting instance: $A=\mathbb Z/2$ and $p_0=(3/4,1/4)$, i.e. the class
$\{(3/4,1/4),(1/4,3/4)\}$ — "the bit is probably $0$" versus "the bit is probably $1$".
Then $C=\tfrac34\log_2 3-1\approx0.189$ bits while the worst-case price is
$\log_2 3-1\approx0.585$ bits: a gap of exactly $\tfrac14\log_2 3\approx0.396$ bits. The
worst-case theory overcharges by a factor of three on two coins.

$C(S\otimes T)=C(S)+C(T)$. There is no universality discount for bundling independent
data — the toll is paid once per independent block, every time.

## 6. Free front ends: the sufficiency criterion

Real compressors never see the raw file. They see a *parse*: a token stream, a
match/literal split, a histogram. Formally the coder sees $f(x)$ for some
coarse-graining $f$. What does that cost?

Coarse-graining never *raises* the price, $C(f_*S)\le C(S)$ — that is data processing.
The exact accounting is a chain rule:

$$D(p\|q)=D(f_*p\|f_*q)+D(p\|q\mid f),$$

where the last term, the **parse defect**, compares the conditional laws *inside the
fibres* of $f$. It is non-negative, and it is exactly the information the front end
discards. The punchline:

> **A front end loses no bits if and only if it computes a sufficient statistic**, i.e.
> if and only if the family factorises as $p_\theta(x)=g_\theta(f(x))\,h(x)$ — the
> [Fisher–Neyman condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufficient_statistic).

That is the test a compressor designer wants: is the histogram enough? Is the
match/literal split enough? Audit your parse below — pick a front end and see whether it
is free or what it costs.

{{interactive_demo:2}}

<details>
<summary><strong>Why the count of ones is free but the parity is not</strong></summary>

For a memoryless binary family, $p_t(x)=t^{\#1(x)}(1-t)^{n-\#1(x)}$ depends on the
message only through its number of ones. So the count *is* the Fisher–Neyman factor:
$g_t(y)=t^y(1-t)^{n-y}$ and $h\equiv1$. Inside a fibre — all messages with the same
count — every source assigns the same conditional law (uniform), so nothing
distinguishes them there, and the defect is zero.

Parity, by contrast, lumps together messages with counts $0,2,4,\dots$. Inside that
fibre a high-bias source concentrates on the large counts and a low-bias source on the
small ones: the conditional laws differ, the defect is positive, and the parse has burnt
the difference. The widget above shows exactly this, fibre by fibre.

</details>

## 7. Rates: what this costs on a real file

Abstract capacity is only useful if it can be computed for the families people actually
compress. Sufficiency does the work.

* **Memoryless (i.i.d.) families** over an alphabet $A$ on messages of length $n$: the
  vector of symbol counts is sufficient, and there are at most $(n+1)^{|A|}$ count
  vectors, so
  $$C\le |A|\log_2(n+1)$$
  *no matter how many sources are in the family*. For binary messages,
  $C\le\log_2(n+1)$.
* **Markov sources** with alphabet $A$: transition counts are sufficient, and
  $$C\le\log_2|A|+|A|^2\log_2(n+1),$$
  where $|A|^2$ is precisely the number of free parameters.

Upper bounds alone are not convincing — perhaps the true price is far smaller. The
matching lower bound is the delicate half, and for the honest one-parameter Bernoulli
family it can be done by an explicit **packing**. Take $k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ and the
biases $t_j=(4j+2)/k$, $j<\lfloor k/4\rfloor$. Under $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(t_j)$ the count
of ones has mean $nt_j$ and variance at most $n/4$, so by Chebyshev at least $15/16$ of
its mass sits within $2\sqrt n$ of the mean; consecutive means are $4\sqrt n$ apart, so
these windows are pairwise **disjoint**. Distinguishable sources are expensive, and one
gets, for every $n\ge64$,

$$\tfrac{15}{32}\log_2 n-8\;\le\;C\;\le\;\log_2(n+1).$$

So the price of a one-parameter family really grows like a constant times $\log_2 n$,
with the constant pinned between $15/32$ and $1$ — bracketing the classical $1/2$. Slide
$n$ below and watch the packing and the bracket together.

## 8. So — are specialised decompressors worth building?

Assemble the pieces. The price of universality over a $d$-parameter family on messages
of length $n$ is $\Theta(\log n)$ bits *in total*, with the constant proportional to $d$.
Merging $K$ specialised classes into one universal scheme costs at most $\log_2 K$ bits,
and never less than the worst specialist:

$$\max_i C_i\;\le\;C(\text{union})\;\le\;B+\log_2 K .$$

{{algorithm:3}}

The verdict is quantitative and slightly deflating. **Specialisation moves only
logarithmically many bits from the message into the shared decompressor.** For a
megabyte file from a modest model class the whole theoretical prize is a few dozen bits
— invisible. It pays in exactly three regimes:

1. **Very short messages**, where $\log_2 n$ is a real fraction of the file;
2. **Many independently coded records**, since the price is additive and the toll is
   paid once per block — a million tiny records pay a million tolls;
3. **Large model families**, where the toll scales with the parameter count.

There is a second, more constructive verdict hidden in Section 6. Since the price depends
only on the sufficient statistic, the productive move is not to ship more specialised
decompressors — it is to find *better parses*. A sufficient front end is free; a
non-sufficient one tells you exactly how many bits it is burning. That is an actionable
design principle, and it comes with a formula.

---

## 9. Coda: the same theorem twice

[Channel capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_capacity) was invented to answer
a question about *transmission*: how fast can you push information down a noisy wire? The
price of universality is a question about *representation*: how many bits do you waste by
not knowing your data?

They are the same number. The family of sources is a channel whose input is the identity
of the source and whose output is the message; its capacity is simultaneously the rate at
which you could signal by choosing a source, and the overhead you pay for not knowing
which source was chosen.

Information you cannot extract and information you must pay for are the same information,
viewed from two sides. That is not a metaphor — it is a theorem, and its proof is a nudge
and a quadratic.

the classical Rissanen rate

constant of the Rissanen rate is bracketed between `15/32` and `1`.

/-! ## The product Bernoulli law and its moments -/

/-- The probability of the binary string `x` under the i.i.d. Bernoulli law with
parameter `t` (probability of `true`). -/
noncomputable def bernProb (t : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → Bool) : ℝ :=
  ∏ i, (if x i then t else 1 - t)

/-- The number of ones in a binary string, as a real number. -/
def onesR {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → Bool) : ℝ := ∑ i, (if x i then (1 : ℝ) else 0)

lemma onesR_eq_ones {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → Bool) : onesR x = (ones x : ℝ) := by
  rw [onesR, ones, Finset.card_filter]
  push_cast
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun i _ => by cases x i <;> simp

lemma bernProb_nonneg {t : ℝ} (h0 : 0 ≤ t) (h1 : t ≤ 1) {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → Bool) :
    0 ≤ bernProb t x :=
  Finset.prod_nonneg fun i _ => by cases x i <;> simp <;> linarith

/-- Splitting a sum over `(Fin (n+1) → Bool)` along the first coordinate. -/
theorem sum_bool_pi_succ (n : ℕ) (F : (Fin (n + 1) → Bool) → ℝ) :
    ∑ x : Fin (n + 1) → Bool, F x
      = (∑ y : Fin n → Bool, F (Fin.cons true y))
        + ∑ y : Fin n → Bool, F (Fin.cons false y) := by
  have h1 : ∑ p : Bool × (Fin n → Bool), F (Fin.cons p.1 p.2)
      = ∑ b : Bool, ∑ y : Fin n → Bool, F (Fin.cons b y) := Fintype.sum_prod_type _
  have h2 : ∑ x : Fin (n + 1) → Bool, F x = ∑ p : Bool × (Fin n → Bool), F (Fin.cons p.1 p.2) :=
    (Fintype.sum_equiv (Fin.consEquiv fun _ => Bool) _ _ fun _ => rfl).symm
  rw [h2, h1, Fintype.sum_bool]

lemma bernProb_cons (t : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (b : Bool) (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    bernProb t (Fin.cons b y) = (if b then t else 1 - t) * bernProb t y := by
  simp [bernProb, Fin.prod_univ_succ]

lemma onesR_cons {n : ℕ} (b : Bool) (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    onesR (Fin.cons b y) = (if b then (1 : ℝ) else 0) + onesR y := by
  rw [onesR, onesR, Fin.sum_univ_succ, Fin.cons_zero]
  simp

lemma bernProb_consT (t : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    bernProb t (Fin.cons true y) = t * bernProb t y := by rw [bernProb_cons]; simp

lemma bernProb_consF (t : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    bernProb t (Fin.cons false y) = (1 - t) * bernProb t y := by rw [bernProb_cons]; simp

lemma onesR_consT {n : ℕ} (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    onesR (Fin.cons true y) = 1 + onesR y := by rw [onesR_cons]; simp

lemma onesR_consF {n : ℕ} (y : Fin n → Bool) :
    onesR (Fin.cons false y) = onesR y := by rw [onesR_cons]; simp

/-- The product Bernoulli law is a probability law (total mass one). -/
theorem bernMoment0 (t : ℝ) (n : ℕ) : ∑ x : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t x = 1 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp [bernProb]
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [sum_bool_pi_succ, Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => bernProb_consT t y),
        Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => bernProb_consF t y), ← Finset.mul_sum,
        ← Finset.mul_sum, ih]
      ring

/-- **First moment**: the expected number of ones is `n t`. -/
theorem bernMoment1 (t : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    ∑ x : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t x * onesR x = n * t := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp [onesR]
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [sum_bool_pi_succ]
      have hT : ∀ y : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t (Fin.cons true y) * onesR (Fin.cons true y)
          = t * (bernProb t y + bernProb t y * onesR y) := by
        intro y; rw [bernProb_consT, onesR_consT]; ring
      have hF : ∀ y : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t (Fin.cons false y) * onesR (Fin.cons false y)
          = (1 - t) * (bernProb t y * onesR y) := by
        intro y; rw [bernProb_consF, onesR_consF]; ring
      rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => hT y), Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => hF y),
        ← Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.mul_sum, Finset.sum_add_distrib, bernMoment0, ih]
      push_cast; ring

/-- **Second moment**: `E[(#ones)²] = n t + n(n−1) t²`. -/
theorem bernMoment2 (t : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    ∑ x : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t x * (onesR x) ^ 2 = n * t + ((n : ℝ) * n - n) * t ^ 2 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp [onesR]
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [sum_bool_pi_succ]
      have hT : ∀ y : Fin n → Bool,
          bernProb t (Fin.cons true y) * (onesR (Fin.cons true y)) ^ 2
            = t * (bernProb t y + 2 * (bernProb t y * onesR y)
                + bernProb t y * (onesR y) ^ 2) := by
        intro y; rw [bernProb_consT, onesR_consT]; ring
      have hF : ∀ y : Fin n → Bool,
          bernProb t (Fin.cons false y) * (onesR (Fin.cons false y)) ^ 2
            = (1 - t) * (bernProb t y * (onesR y) ^ 2) := by
        intro y; rw [bernProb_consF, onesR_consF]; ring
      rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => hT y), Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun y _ => hF y),
        ← Finset.mul_sum, Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_add_distrib,
        bernMoment0, ← Finset.mul_sum, bernMoment1, ih, ← Finset.mul_sum, ih]
      push_cast; ring

/-- **The variance of the binomial count**, proved from scratch:
`∑ₓ p(x) (#ones(x) − n t)² = n t (1 − t)`. -/
theorem bernVariance (t : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :
    ∑ x : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t x * (onesR x - n * t) ^ 2 = n * t * (1 - t) := by
  have h : ∀ x : Fin n → Bool, bernProb t x * (onesR x - n * t) ^ 2
      = bernProb t x * (onesR x) ^ 2 - (2 * ((n : ℝ) * t)) * (bernProb t x * onesR x)
        + ((n : ℝ) * t) ^ 2 * bernProb t x := by
    intro x; ring
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun x _ => h x), Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_sub_distrib,
    ← Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.mul_sum, bernMoment0, bernMoment1, bernMoment2]
  ring

/-! ## Chebyshev's inequality in the finite setting -/

/-- **Chebyshev bound for the number of ones.**  The window of half-width `c`
around the mean `n t` carries mass at least `1 − n t (1−t) / c²`. -/
theorem bern_window_mass_ge {t : ℝ} (h0 : 0 ≤ t) (h1 : t ≤ 1) (n : ℕ) {c : ℝ} (hc : 0 < c) :
    1 - (n : ℝ) * t * (1 - t) / c ^ 2
      ≤ ∑ x ∈ univ.filter (fun x : Fin n → Bool => |onesR x - n * t| < c), bernProb t x := by
  classical
  set P : (Fin n → Bool) → Prop := fun x => |onesR x - n * t| < c with hP
  have hsplit :
      (∑ x ∈ univ.filter P, bernProb t x) + ∑ x ∈ univ.filter (fun x => ¬ P x), bernProb t x
        = 1 := by
    rw [Finset.sum_filter_add_sum_filter_not, bernMoment0]
  -- the tail is small
  have htail : (∑ x ∈ univ.filter (fun x => ¬ P x), bernProb t x) * c ^ 2
      ≤ (n : ℝ) * t * (1 - t) := by
    have hstep : ∀ x ∈ univ.filter (fun x => ¬ P x),
        bernProb t x * c ^ 2 ≤ bernProb t x * (onesR x - n * t) ^ 2 := by
      intro x hx
      have hxn : ¬ |onesR x - n * t| < c := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hx).2
      have hge : c ≤ |onesR x - n * t| := le_of_not_gt hxn
      have hsq : c ^ 2 ≤ (onesR x - n * t) ^ 2 := by
        have habs : |onesR x - (n : ℝ) * t| ^ 2 = (onesR x - (n : ℝ) * t) ^ 2 :=
          sq_abs _
        nlinarith [hge, hc.le, abs_nonneg (onesR x - (n : ℝ) * t)]
